sources.title: NGSS MS-ESS2-6: Develop and use a model to describe how unequal heating and rotation of the Earth cause patterns of atmospheric and oceanic circulation that determine regional climates
NOAA National Ocean Service: Surface Ocean Currents (trade winds and westerlies)

note.text: The sun heats Earth unevenly: most strongly near the equator, least at the poles.

steps.title: Latitude lines
steps.instruction: Draw the equator and the lines at 30° and 60°.

note.text: Hot air rises at the equator, sinks near 30°, and rises again near 60°. This makes three loops of air in each half of Earth.

steps.title: Trade winds
steps.instruction: Draw the four arrows between the equator and 30°.

note.text: Air sinking near 30° flows back toward the equator. Earth's spin bends it, so these trade winds blow from the east.
note.remember: Trade winds: 0° to 30°, from the east.

steps.title: Westerlies
steps.instruction: Draw the four arrows between 30° and 60°.

note.text: Between about 35° and 60°, the westerlies blow from west to east. Air rising near 60° brings rainy, stormy weather.

steps.title: Polar easterlies
steps.instruction: Draw the arrows near the poles.

note.text: Cold air sinks at the poles and spreads out as the polar easterlies, blowing from the east.

steps.title: Name the winds
steps.instruction: Pick the name of each numbered wind belt.

mistakes.Westerlies: These blow from the east, toward the equator. They're the trade winds.

mistakes.Trade winds: These blow from the west, between 30° and 60°: the westerlies.

steps.title: Climate
steps.question: Many of the world's deserts lie near 30° north and south. Why?

options.text: Sinking air there makes high pressure, which brings dry, clear weather
options.feedback: Yes. Sinking air forms a belt of high pressure, and high pressure usually means fair, dry weather.

options.text: It's the hottest place on Earth
options.feedback: The equator gets the most direct sunlight. Deserts near 30° come from sinking, dry air.
Winds blow there. The dryness comes from air sinking and forming high pressure.

options.text: The ocean is too far away
options.feedback: Some of these deserts are on coasts. The cause is sinking air and high pressure.

steps.title: Causes
steps.question: Which two things cause the pattern of wind belts?

options.text: Uneven heating by the sun, and Earth's rotation
options.feedback: Right. Uneven heating sets air moving between the equator and poles; Earth's spin bends it into east and west winds.

options.text: The moon's gravity and the tides
options.feedback: Tides don't make the wind belts. The sun's uneven heating and Earth's spin do.
Land shapes local winds, but the global belts come from uneven heating and Earth's spin.
Rotation bends the winds, but uneven heating by the sun is what sets the air moving.
